source_text: I. De Liberi Arbitrii natura & essentia multas quaestiones movent, & inter se agitant Doctores Scholae Romanae; quae tamen potius ad Metaphysicos, quam ad Theologos pertinent: neque omnes hic recensere & excutere est animus; sed ea solum breviter attingere quae aliquo modo spectant ad eas controversias quibus hodie fervent, & super quibus inter se digladiantur Scholae Christianae.
english: The teachers of the Roman School debate many questions among themselves about what free choice is and what makes it what it is. Most of these belong more to metaphysics than to theology, and there is no intention here of listing and sifting them all.
Only those will be touched, and briefly, that bear somehow on the controversies now inflaming the Christian schools and dividing them against one another.

source_text: II. Omittimus igitur ea quae disputare solent circa liberi Arbitrii genus, an, scilicet, sit actus, habitus, vel potentia, & ad quid eorum quae sunt in anima revocari debeat. Quanquam enim veteres nonnulli docuerint liberum arbitrium neque in potentia quadam, neque etiam in habitu aliquo consistere, sed potius in actu quodam, quam sententiam tribuit Bellarminus Herveo Theologo sententiario: alii vero existimaverint liberum arbitrium non esse actum, neque potentiam, sed habitum quendam naturalem consurgentem ex intellectu & voluntate, quam sententiam tenuit Bonaventura Cardinalis, & in Schola Romana Doctor Celeberrimus, nihilominus in eo jam tota Schola Romana consentit, liberum Arbitrium esse potentiam quandam & facultatem.
english: The usual disputes about the genus of free choice are passed over here: whether it is an act, a habit, or a power, and under which of the soul's contents it should be classed.

Some older writers did teach that free choice lies not in a power or a habit but in an act; Bellarmine assigns that view to Hervaeus, the commentator on the Sentences. Others held that it is neither act nor power but a natural habit arising from intellect and will, which was the view of Cardinal Bonaventure, a teacher of great fame in the Roman School.
Even so, the whole Roman School now agrees that free choice is a power and a faculty.

source_text: III. Rursus posito quod liberum Arbitrium sit potentia quaedam, quaesitum est quae sit illa potentia, neque de hac re omnibus idem visum. Thomas & Bonaventura teste Bellarmino, referunt nonnullos sensisse liberum arbitrium non esse unicam & particularem animae potentiam, sed potius potentiam quandam universalem, quae sub se tanquam species complectatur omnes potentias animae, tum sentientis, tum intelligentis, quae actus quomodocunque liberos edunt. Alii vero ut Alexander Halensis Scholasticus nobilis ipsius Thomae Aquinatis & Bonaventurae praeceptor, dixerunt liberum arbitrium esse quidem potentiam quandam particularem, sed quae sit ab intellectu & voluntate distincta. Verum quaestio ista praetermitti quoque potest, quandoquidem in eo jam consentiunt omnes Scholae quod liberum arbitrium non sit quid ab intellectu & voluntate reapse distinctum.
english: Once free choice was granted to be a power, the next question was which power it is, and opinions differed.

Thomas and Bonaventure, on Bellarmine's testimony, report that some took it to be not one particular power of the soul but a universal power containing as its species every power of the soul, sentient or intellectual, that produces acts free in any way.
Others, such as Alexander of Hales, the noble scholastic who taught both Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, called it a particular power but one distinct from intellect and will.
This question too can be left aside, for all the schools now agree that free choice is not anything really distinct from intellect and will.

source_text: IV. Sed ulterius quaeritur an liberum arbitrium utraque facultate constet, & an utraque ad ipsum pertineat, An vero sit ad solam voluntatem restringendum. Nonnulli, ut Durandus in Schola Romana Doctor magni nominis, existimaverunt liberum Arbitrium facultatem utramque complecti, mentem, scilicet, atque voluntatem: neque voluntatem solam, sed etiam rationem esse formaliter, ut loquuntur, liberam: imo libertatem prius & magis convenire rationi quam voluntati.
english: A further question is whether free choice is made up of both faculties and belongs to both, or must be confined to the will alone.

Some held that it includes both mind and will. Durandus, a teacher of high standing in the Roman School, was of this view. He said that reason, and not the will only, is free 'formally', to use their term, and indeed that freedom belongs to reason first and more fully than to the will.

source_text: V. Ad quam sententiam accedit Petrus Gassendus Vir Celeberrimus Ecclesiae Diniensis in Provincia praepositus, tractatu de libertate, Fortuna & Fato, qui habetur in fine tomi secundi operum ipsius. Ubi dicit sibi videri libertatem in intellectu esse primo & per se, in voluntate autem secundario, & dependenter. Fundamentum autem illius est, quod cum ex communiori Scholae Romanae sensu, ut jam jam videbitur, libertas sita sit in quadam potestatis liberae indifferentia & indeterminatione, ratio indifferens est in judicando de rebus agendis, & de illis potest hoc, vel illo modo judicare; adeoque quicquid est in voluntate indifferentiae in rebus appetendis, ex hac quae in ratione est indifferentia oritur. Quod enim voluntas potest unum & idem objectum respuere, vel amplecti, & inter varia objecta istud, vel illud eligere, inde est quod ratio varia de objectis illis judicia ferre potest, prout diversae boni, vel mali rationes, in iis illi se offerunt.
english: Pierre Gassendi, a man of great renown and provost of the church of Digne in Provence, adopts this view in his treatise on freedom, fortune, and fate, printed at the end of the second volume of his works. There he says freedom seems to him to be in the intellect first and in its own right, and in the will only secondarily and by dependence.

His ground is this. On the more common Roman view, as will shortly appear, freedom lies in a certain indifference and indeterminacy of a free power. Reason is indifferent when it judges what is to be done and can judge it one way or another, so any indifference the will has toward things it desires springs from the indifference in reason.

The will can refuse or accept one and the same object, and pick this or that among many. It can do so because reason can form different judgments of those objects as different aspects of good or evil appear in them.

source_text: VI. Porro mentem quovis respectu liberam esse non vult, sed tantum quatenus ad objecta plurima indifferenter quodammodo se habet, & sua natura ita flexilis est, ut verum pro objecto habens, possit nunc unum nunc aliud judicare de quapiam re, & nunc unum, nunc aliud judicium de ipsa pro vero habere: licet non possit ab eo quod verum apparet dissentire, nec ei quod falsum videtur assentiri, neque etiam de re aliqua judicium mutare, nisi ex parte objecti sese offerat major, vel minor species sive veri, sive falsi. Adeo ut intellectum humanum comparet librae, quae modo in hanc, modo in illam partem inclinatur, prout isti, vel illi lanci, aliquid ponderis accedit, vel decedit: & cujus altera Lanx semel depressa non potest attolli, nisi Lanci oppositae aliquid ponderis addatur, prout ista latius diducta videre est apud Virum illum Clarissimum tomo supra citato pag. 82.
english: He does not make the mind free in every respect. It is free only in that it stands somewhat indifferently toward a great many objects and is so pliable by nature that, while its object is truth, it can judge a matter now one way and now another and take now this judgment and now that one for true.
Yet it cannot refuse what appears true or accept what seems false. Nor can it change its judgment of anything unless the object presents a stronger or weaker appearance of truth or falsehood.

He therefore likens the human intellect to a pair of scales that tilts one way or the other as weight is added to or taken from either pan. Once one pan has gone down, it cannot rise again unless weight is put on the other.
The illustrious author develops this at greater length in the same volume, page 82.

source_text: VII. Verum haec sententia communiter in Schola Romana rejicitur. Nam plerique illius Doctores existimant intellectum non esse formaliter liberum, sed libertatem esse per se & formaliter in sola voluntate. Ac proinde docent liberum arbitrium non esse potentiam a voluntate diversam, nec aliud quam ipsam voluntatem, certo tamen respectu & modo consideratam: ita ut quamvis voluntas & liberum arbitrium sint potentia reapse eadem, nihilominus Liberum Arbitrium a voluntate sit ratione distinctum.
english: The Roman School, however, generally rejects this view. Most of its teachers hold that the intellect is not free formally, and that freedom belongs in its own right and formally to the will alone.

So they teach that free choice is no power other than the will. It is simply the will, regarded in a certain respect and manner. The will and free choice are thus one and the same power in reality, yet free choice is distinguished from the will by a distinction of reason.

source_text: VIII. Etenim ex eorum mente voluntas latius patet quam liberum Arbitrium & quoad objecta, & quoad actiones. Nam quaecunque fiunt a libero arbitrio eadem quoque a voluntate fiunt, sed non contra. Et quicquid objectum est Liberi Arbitrii objectum est quoque voluntatis, sed non quicquid est objectum voluntatis est etiam liberi arbitrii objectum. Quippe finis summus, id est, beatitudo est objectum voluntatis, sed non est objectum liberi arbitrii, ad cujus objectum pertinent tantum media ad finem. Unde fit ut illi actus, quibus volumus esse felices, & nolumus esse miseri, sint actiones voluntatis, sed non actiones liberi arbitrii: quia voluntas in ultimum finem non fertur libere sed naturaliter.
english: In their view the will covers more ground than free choice, both in its objects and in its acts. Everything done by free choice is also done by the will, but the reverse does not hold.

Likewise every object of free choice is an object of the will, but not every object of the will falls to free choice. The highest end, happiness, is an object of the will, whereas free choice has for its object only the means to that end.
It follows that the acts by which we want to be happy and do not want to be wretched are acts of the will and not of free choice, since the will moves toward the last end by nature and not freely.

source_text: IX. Porro quamvis Theologi Scholastici communiter statuant intellectum non esse liberum per se & formaliter, agnoscunt tamen in eo esse radicem & causam, saltem sine qua non, libertatis illius quae est in voluntate: quae, scilicet, ex eo nascitur quod intellectus humanus non tantum varia objecta voluntati proponat, sed ea quoque inter se comparet; ac in uno & eodem objecto varias boni & mali rationes percipiat, & voluntati quodammodo demonstret. Unde fit ut voluntas possit unum & idem objectum respuere, vel amplecti, & inter objecta varia istud, vel illud eligere: qua in re positum est libertatis exercitium.
english: The scholastic theologians generally say the intellect is not free in itself and formally. Still they grant that it holds the root and cause of the will's freedom, at the least as the condition without which there would be none.

That freedom arises because the human intellect does more than set different objects before the will. It also weighs them against each other, sees different aspects of good and evil in a single object, and in a manner points them out to the will.
That is why the will can refuse or accept the same object and choose this or that among many, and in this the use of freedom consists.

source_text: X. Ut vero negent intellectum esse formaliter liberum, eo praecipue moventur quod bene, vel male moraliter agere proprium est ejus facultatis quae formaliter & per se libera est. Virtus autem & vitium proprie, ut ipsis videtur, ad solam voluntatem pertinent; neque ulla actio laudem, vel vituperium, praemium, vel poenam meretur, nisi quatenus a voluntate procedit. Adeo ut ipsius intellectus operationes peccati & meriti rationem non habeant, nisi in quantum voluntariae sunt, & certo quodam modo a voluntate imperantur.
english: Their main reason for denying the intellect formal freedom is that acting morally well or badly belongs to the faculty that is free formally and in itself.
In their judgment virtue and vice belong strictly to the will alone. No action deserves praise or blame, reward or punishment, except as it comes from the will.
Hence even the intellect's own operations count as sin or merit only so far as they are voluntary and in some fashion directed by the will.

source_text: XI. Quod autem videtur in hac quaestione praecipuum, illud est in quo proprie posita sit, illa libertas a qua voluntas libera dicitur, & in qua consistit ratio liberi arbitrii. Qua de re non omnino convenit inter Theologos Ecclesiae Romanae. Sed ut discrepantes eorum sententiae melius intelligi possint, primum tenendum est quae sint in Scholis usitatae libertatis acceptiones atque distinctiones.
english: The central point of the question appears to be where, strictly, the freedom lies that makes the will called free and in which the essence of free choice consists.
Theologians of the Roman Church are not entirely agreed on this. To make their differing opinions clearer, one must first set out the senses and distinctions of freedom that the schools employ.

source_text: XII. Libertas ergo opponitur 1. Servituti, 2. Coactioni, 3. Necessitati. Rursus vero servitus & proinde illi opposita libertas est propria vel Metaphorica. Proprie dicta servitus est illa qua qui sunt inter homines conditione servi, sunt in Dominorum suorum potestate. Metaphorica vero servitus est, quum Dominium in homines figurate rebus quibusdam tribuitur. Ut quum homines peccatis indulgentes dicuntur in scriptura esse peccati servi, & qui per justam Dei sententiam sunt exitio & morti addicti, similiter dicuntur servi mortis & corruptionis. Illi vero servituti qua homines sunt peccato mancipati opponitur alia servitus, nempe servitus justitiae, quae est libertas a peccato, sive libertas gratiae, ut vocatur in Scholis. Et servituti miseriae, sive mortis & corruptionis, opponit scriptura libertatem quam vocat gloriae filiorum Dei.
english: Freedom, then, stands over against three things: servitude, compulsion, and necessity.

Servitude, and with it the opposing freedom, is either literal or figurative. Literal servitude is the state of people who are slaves by legal condition and so are under their masters' power. Figurative servitude is when something is spoken of as lord over men.
Thus Scripture calls those who give themselves to their sins slaves of sin, and those whom God's just sentence has handed over to ruin and death are likewise called slaves of death and decay.

Against the slavery to sin Scripture sets another servitude, that of righteousness, which is freedom from sin; the schools call it the freedom of grace. Against the slavery of misery, that is, of death and decay, Scripture sets what it calls the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

source_text: XIII. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae notant libertatem de qua hic agitur, & a qua denominatur liberum arbitrium, non esse libertatem illam quae opponitur servituti, seu propriae seu Metaphoricae. Idque quoniam homines conditione servi non propterea carent libero Arbitrio; Neque etiam per peccatum eo spoliati sunt illi quos scriptura sacra vocat peccati servos.
english: The teachers of the Roman Church point out that the freedom under discussion, from which free choice takes its name, is not the freedom opposed to servitude, either literal or figurative.
Someone who is a slave by condition is not for that reason without free choice. Neither have those whom Scripture calls slaves of sin been robbed of it by sin.

source_text: XIV. Nulli quoque dubium est quin libertas de qua hic, coactionem maxime excludat; sed quaeritur an soli coactioni opponatur, non etiam necessitati; & an ad eam sufficiat in agente rationali, immunitas a coactione? Et quidem non pauci inter veteres Scholasticos in ea videntur fuisse sententia libertatem arbitrii in genere consideratam, oppositam non esse necessitati simpliciter, sed coactioni tantum.
english: Nobody questions that this freedom shuts out compulsion before all else. The question is whether compulsion is the only thing it excludes, or necessity as well, and whether in a rational agent it is enough to be exempt from compulsion.
In fact a fair number of the older scholastics seem to have held that freedom of choice, taken in general, is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

source_text: XV. Ita procul omni dubio censuit Bonaventura, cujus haec verba sunt in secundum sententiarum distinct. 7. quaest. 2. Ad illud quod dicitur quod libere velle, & necessario opponuntur, dicendum quod duplex est necessitas, quaedam a causa extrinseca, utpote necessitas coactionis: & haec opponitur ei quod est libere velle. Quaedam vero est a dispositione intrinseca, & haec huic non opponitur: imo stat simul cum libertate. Talis est in libero arbitrio daemonum, qui ita conglutinant sibi malum, ut nullo modo velint ab eo separari. Et distinctione vigesima quinta quaest. 2. Liberum arbitrium, inquit, dupliciter potest considerari: aut secundum quod liberum est, aut secundum quod deliberans. Si loquamur de ipso secundum quod liberum, sic concedo quod potest esse non solum respectu contingentis, sed etiam necessarii, sicut patet in Deo, & in Christo, & in Angelis, & in hominibus beatis. Cum enim duplex sit necessitas, videlicet, coactionis & immutabilitatis, necessitas coactionis repugnat libertati arbitrii, non autem necessitas immutabilitatis: eo quod arbitrium dicitur liberum, non quia sic velit hoc ut possit velle ejus oppositum, sed quia omne quod vult appetit ad sui ipsius imperium, quia sic vult aliquid, ut velit se velle illud, & ideo in actu volendi seipsum movet, & sibi dominatur, & pro tanto dicitur liberum, quamvis immutabiliter ordinetur ad illud. Et paulo inferius, Actus liberi arbitrii, ut liberum est, non solum potest esse circa necessarium, sed etiam necessarius in se.
english: Bonaventure plainly held this view. On the second book of the Sentences, distinction 7, question 2, he writes: 'To the claim that willing freely and willing necessarily are opposed, the answer is that necessity is of two kinds. One comes from an outside cause, such as the necessity of compulsion, and this is opposed to willing freely. The other comes from an inner disposition, and this is not opposed to it but stands together with freedom. Such is the necessity in the free choice of the demons, who bind evil to themselves so tightly that they would by no means be parted from it.'

In distinction 25, question 2, he says: 'Free choice may be considered in two ways, as free or as deliberating. Taken as free, I grant that it can concern not only what is contingent but also what is necessary, as is evident in God, in Christ, in the angels, and in the blessed.

'There are two necessities, of compulsion and of immutability. The first conflicts with freedom of choice, the second does not. For choice is called free not because, in willing this, it can will the opposite, but because whatever it wills it seeks under its own command. It wills a thing in such a way that it wills itself to will it, and so in the very act of willing it moves itself and rules itself. For that reason it is called free, even though it is unchangeably directed to its object.'
A little later he adds: 'The act of free choice, taken as free, can not only concern what is necessary but can itself be necessary.'

source_text: XVI. Atque hanc doctrinam ab institutore suo Alexandro de Hales hauserat Bonaventura. Is enim pluribus in locis libertatem essentialem liberi arbitrii constituit in libertate a coactione. Praesertim vero haec sunt illius verba. Duplex est necessitas inevitabilitatis & coactionis. Necessitas coactionis tollit liberum arbitrium, sed non necessitas inevitabilitatis, licet ergo in angelis sit necessitas inevitabilitatis, nihilominus tamen est liberum arbitrium, 2. p. q. 72. memb. 3. art. 3.
english: Bonaventure learned this teaching from his master, Alexander of Hales, who in many places makes the essential freedom of free choice consist in freedom from compulsion.

His clearest statement runs: 'Necessity is of two kinds, of inevitability and of compulsion. The necessity of compulsion destroys free choice; the necessity of inevitability does not. So although there is a necessity of inevitability in the angels, they still have free choice.' (Summa, part 2, q. 72, memb. 3, art. 3.)

source_text: XVII. Eandem etiam doctrinam secutus est, ejusdem Alexandri Halensis Discipulus alter, Thomas Aquinas. Nam naturalis necessitas, inquit, secundum quam voluntas aliquid ex necessitate velle dicitur ut felicitatem, libertati non repugnat, ut Augustinus docet in primo de civitate Dei. Libertas enim voluntatis violentiae, vel coactioni opponitur. Non est autem violentia, vel coactio in hoc quod aliquid secundum ordinem suae naturae movetur; sed magis in hoc quod naturalis motus impeditur: sicut cum impeditur grave ne descendat ad medium. Unde voluntas libere appetit felicitatem, licet necessario appetat illam. Sic autem & Deus sua voluntate libere amat seipsum, licet de necessitate amet seipsum. quaest. 10. de Potent. art. 2. ad 1.
english: Thomas Aquinas, another pupil of the same Alexander of Hales, held the same doctrine. 'Natural necessity,' he says, 'by which the will is said to will something necessarily, happiness for instance, does not conflict with freedom, as Augustine teaches in the first book of The City of God.

'Freedom of the will is opposed to violence or compulsion. There is no violence or compulsion when a thing moves according to the order of its own nature. Violence lies rather in hindering a natural motion, as when a heavy body is kept from falling toward the center.

'So the will seeks happiness freely, though it seeks it necessarily. In the same way God too loves himself freely by his will, even though he loves himself of necessity.' (De potentia, q. 10, art. 2, ad 1.)

source_text: XVIII. Hinc est quod docet opus quoddam esse posse laude, vel vituperio dignum, meritorium, vel demeritorium, ex hoc quod est spontaneum non coactum & voluntarium, tametsi voluntas illius respectu sit ad unum determinata. Nam in tertium sententiarum scribens, [marg.: Dist. 12. q. 2. art. 1. ad 3.] Impotentia coactionis, inquit, quae opponitur voluntario, tollit rationem meriti & demeriti, non impotentia quae est ex perfectione in bonitate, vel malitia, quia hoc voluntarium non tollit, sed ponit voluntatem confirmatam ad unum. Et in eodem libro, ut explicaret quomodo Christus mereri potuerit per liberum arbitrium determinatum ad unum numero, scilicet ad diligendum Deum: [marg.: Dist. 18. art. 2. ad 5.] Dicendum, inquit, quod etiamsi esset determinatum ad unum numero sicut ad diligendum Deum, quod non facere non potest: tamen ex hoc, non amittit libertatem, aut rationem laudis, sive meriti, quia in illud non coacte, sed sponte tendit, & ita est actus sui Dominus.
english: So he teaches that a deed may deserve praise or blame, merit or demerit, simply because it is spontaneous, voluntary, and not forced, even though the will is fixed on that one thing.

On the third book of the Sentences (margin: dist. 12, q. 2, art. 1, ad 3) he writes: 'The inability that comes from compulsion, which is the opposite of the voluntary, removes merit and demerit. Not so the inability that comes from perfection in good or in evil. That does not remove the voluntary; it presupposes a will confirmed in one direction.'

In the same book (margin: dist. 18, art. 2, ad 5) he explains how Christ could merit by a free choice fixed on one single act, namely the love of God: 'Even if it were fixed on one single act, such as loving God, which it cannot fail to do, it does not on that account lose its freedom or its claim to praise or merit. It goes toward that act spontaneously and not under force, and so remains in command of its act.'

source_text: XIX. Neque hac in parte diversa est ipsius Scoti doctrina. Etenim tria haec circa libertatem voluntatis clare & aperte docet. 1. Libertatem voluntatis omnino consistere posse cum necessitate. Quippe haec sunt illius verba, Cum necessitate ad volendum stat libertas in voluntate. Nam in eo est libertas volendi, quia delectabiliter & eligibiliter elicit actum, & permanet in actu. 2. Voluntatem, sive necessario, sive contingenter agat, semper agere libere, nunquam naturaliter. Voluntas, inquit, semper habet suum modum causandi proprium, scilicet, libere. Et rursum, voluntas ut voluntas, est principium activum libere. Non magis igitur voluntas potest esse naturaliter activa quam natura, ut est principium distinctum contra voluntatem, potest esse libere activa. 3. Non solum in creaturis, sed & in ipso Deo hoc habere locum, quod & ipse diligat seipsum liberrime, quamvis necessaria voluntate. Voluntas divina, inquit, necessario vult bonitatem suam, & tamen in volendo eam est libera. Quodlib. 16. ut citat Jansenius in suo Augustino, De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 6. cap. 25.
english: Scotus does not differ on this point. He teaches three things about the will's freedom clearly and openly.

First, the will's freedom is fully compatible with necessity: 'Freedom remains in the will together with necessity of willing. For freedom of willing lies in this, that the will brings forth its act with delight and by choice and continues in it.'

Second, whether the will acts necessarily or contingently, it always acts freely and never by nature: 'The will always has its own manner of causing, namely freely.' Again: 'The will as will is a principle that acts freely. So the will can no more act by nature than nature, taken as a principle set over against will, can act freely.'

Third, this holds not only in creatures but in God himself, who loves himself with the greatest freedom though with a necessary will: 'The divine will necessarily wills its own goodness, and yet in willing it, it is free.' (Quodlibet 16, as cited by Jansenius in his Augustinus, On the Grace of Christ the Saviour, book 6, chapter 25.)

source_text: XX. Porro ista scholae lumina insequentibus proxime seculis secuti sunt alii magno numero Scholastici, ut Thomas de Argentina juxta quem Necessitas coactionis tollit rationem meriti, necessitas immutabilitatis proveniens ex perfectione virtutum non tollit, sed auget. Marsilius ab Inghen ex cujus sententia Necessarium & inevitabile, non per naturam, sed per gratiam, non tollit rationem laudabilis. Gabriel Biel secundum quem Actus beatitudinis est libere elicitus, & ita contingens etsi immutabilis & perpetuus. Libere, inquam, complacenter, licet non libere contradictorie, quae libertas sufficit ad rationem meriti. Nicolaus de Orbellis cujus haec verba sunt a Bonaventura desumpta, Dicitur liberum arbitrium simpliciter, non quod sic velit hoc ut possit velle oppositum, sed quia omne quod vult appetit ad sui ipsius imperium, quia sic vult aliquid ut velit se velle illud, & ideo in actu volendi seipsum movet, & sibi dominatur; & pro tanto dicitur liberum, quamvis immutabiliter ordinetur ad illud. Denique Stephanus Brulefer qui docet quod Actus liberi Arbitrii deliberantis, quamvis possit esse circa necessarium, semper est contingens. Actus vero liberi Arbitrii, ut liberum est, non solum potest esse circa necessarium, sed etiam necessarius in se. Quorum omnium, & plurium aliorum loca prolixe citata videre licet apud jam dictum Jansenium libro illo sexto de gratia Salvatoris cap. 29. & sequentibus.
english: These luminaries of the school were followed in the centuries just after them by a great many other scholastics.

Thomas of Strasbourg says: 'The necessity of compulsion removes merit; the necessity of immutability that comes from perfected virtue does not remove it but increases it.' Marsilius of Inghen says: 'What is necessary and inevitable, not by nature but by grace, does not cease to be praiseworthy.'

Gabriel Biel says: 'The act of blessedness is freely brought forth, and so is contingent though unchangeable and everlasting. It is free, I mean, by consent and delight, though not free to do the contrary, and that freedom is enough for merit.'

Nicholas de Orbellis borrows Bonaventure's words: free choice is called free simply, not because in willing one thing it can will the opposite, but because whatever it wills it seeks under its own command. It wills something in such a way that it wills itself to will it, so that in the act of willing it moves and rules itself, and for that reason it is called free even though it is unchangeably directed to its object.

Finally Stephen Brulefer teaches: 'The act of free choice as deliberating, though it may concern what is necessary, is always contingent. But the act of free choice as free can not only concern what is necessary but can itself be necessary.'
All these passages, and many more, are quoted at length by Jansenius in the sixth book on the grace of the Saviour, chapter 29 and following.

source_text: XXI. Imo sententiam istam superiori saeculo in Schola Rom. retinuerunt adhuc Theologi nonnulli. Ut Alfonsus de Castro ordinis Minorum lib. de haeresibus in verbo Libertas. Est, inquit, adhuc Alia libertas quae opponitur necessitati, vel ut verius dicam coactioni. Et subjungit, quando dicimus hominis arbitrium esse liberum, istud intelligi de hac libertate. Alfonsi vero verba postea adoptavit & sua fecit Joseph Angles, designatus Episcopus Bosanensis, ex ordine quoque Minorum, in secundum librum sententiarum scribens. Nam postquam loquutus est de libertate gratiae & libertate gloriae, Tertio, inquit, est libertas, quae opponitur necessitati, vel, ut verius dicam, coactioni. Et haec est libertas naturae, de qua loquimur in praesentia. Et postea, ubi distinxit triplicem libertatem, Unam a coactione, Alteram a peccato, Tertiam a miseria, haec est illius Conclusio, Quoad libertatem primo modo, aeque in homine & in Angelo est liberum Arbitrium: Et ratio est, quia neque mali Angeli, neque boni, neque mali hominis voluntas cogi potest. In sequentibus vero postquam proposuit quaestionem illam, Utrum Actus liberi Arbitrii sit contingentium tantum, vel etiam necessariorum, Observat ex Bonaventura, liberum arbitrium posse dupliciter considerari, vel quatenus liberum est, vel quatenus deliberans est. Deinde subjungit duas conclusiones. 1. Actus liberi arbitrii potest esse, & est necessariorum. Ratio est, quia in Deo, angelis & in hominibus beatis, est liberum arbitrium, quod quidem immutabiliter, & necessario in suum actum exit; quia Deus per naturam, & Angelus & homo beatus per gloriam, immutabilis est. II. Si liberum Arbitrium secundo modo accipiatur, actus illius contingentium est. Ratio est, quia non consiliamur, neque consultamus de necessariis, & impossibilibus, sed de contingentibus, quae facere vel non facere in nostra potestate situm est. Ad distinctionem 24. & 25. quaest. unica de Libero Arbitrio art. 1. 2. & 3.
english: Even in the last century some theologians of the Roman School still held this view. Alfonso de Castro, a Franciscan, writes in his book on heresies under the heading Liberty: 'There is yet another freedom, opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion.' He adds that when we call man's choice free, it is this freedom that is meant.

Joseph Angles, another Franciscan and bishop-designate of Bosa, later took over Alfonso's words as his own in his commentary on the second book of the Sentences. Having spoken of the freedom of grace and the freedom of glory, he says: 'Third, there is the freedom opposed to necessity, or more accurately to compulsion. This is the freedom of nature, which is our present subject.'

Later, after distinguishing freedom from compulsion, from sin, and from misery, he concludes: 'As regards freedom in the first sense, free choice exists equally in men and in angels. The reason is that the will of neither bad nor good angels, nor of bad men, can be forced.'

Further on he asks whether the act of free choice concerns only contingent things or necessary things as well. Following Bonaventure, he notes that free choice may be viewed either as free or as deliberating, and he draws two conclusions.

First: 'The act of free choice can concern and does concern necessary things. For there is free choice in God, in the angels, and in the blessed, and it issues in its act unchangeably and necessarily, since God is unchangeable by nature and angels and the blessed by glory.'

Second: 'If free choice is taken in the second sense, its act concerns contingent things. For we do not deliberate or take counsel about what is necessary or impossible, but about contingent things that it is in our power to do or leave undone.' (On distinctions 24 and 25, the single question on free choice, arts. 1-3.)

source_text: XXII. Caeterum Doctores illi, ut facile colligi potest ex illis ipsis quae hactenus citata sunt, quando affirmant libertatem Arbitrii oppositam esse, non necessitati simpliciter, sed potius coactioni, per id significatum nolunt, naturam & essentiam libertatis consistere in eo quod agens est a coactione immune, ut supponere videntur qui contra eos disputant. Fatentur enim multa agere non coacte, neque tamen libere. Quippe nullum agens ipsis liberum est nisi illud quod agit ex intellectus judicio. Sed istud tantum sibi volunt in eo qui agit ex judicio rationis, solam coactionem libertatem perimere, non vero necessitatem. Et esse quidem impossibile ut quis simul coacte, & tamen libere agat; sed posse fieri ut aliquis agat libere, quanquam necessario.
english: As the passages already quoted readily show, these teachers say that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but to compulsion. They do not mean, as their opponents seem to assume, that the nature and essence of freedom is simply exemption from compulsion.
They admit that many things act without being forced and yet do not act freely, for in their view nothing is a free agent unless it acts on the judgment of the intellect.

Their point is narrower. In one who acts on the judgment of reason, compulsion alone destroys freedom, and necessity does not. No one can act under force and freely at the same time, but someone can act freely even though he acts necessarily.

source_text: XXIII. Praeterea non est haec eorum sententia, libertati semper esse adjunctam necessitatem, neque liberum arbitrium, praecipue hominis, respectu plerorumque suorum actuum, esse indifferens & indeterminatum. Agnoscunt enim, homines, quamdiu in via sunt, non tantum agere libere, sed ita affectos esse, ut in agendo nulla naturali, sive proprie dicta necessitate teneantur, sed possint agere & ab agendo cessare, agere hoc aut illud, & circa idem objectum contrarios actus exercere. Sed putant libertatem simpliciter consideratam non consistere in ejusmodi ad agendum indifferentia, & indeterminatione, aut eam semper habere comitem; verum absque illa posse manere & conservari, & quandoque etiam in eo reperiri, qui nullo modo est ad agendum indifferens, sed inevitabiliter & immutabiliter agit.
english: Nor do they hold that freedom always comes with necessity, or that free choice, especially in man, is not indifferent and undetermined with regard to most of its acts.

They grant that people in this present life not only act freely but are so constituted that no natural necessity, or necessity strictly so called, binds them in acting. They can act or stop, do this or that, and perform opposite acts toward the same object.

What they deny is that freedom, considered simply, consists in that indifference and indeterminacy toward action or always goes with it. Freedom can remain and be kept without it, and it is sometimes found in one who is not indifferent at all but acts inevitably and unchangeably.

source_text: XXIV. Nam praeter libertatem illam quae in scholis vocatur, Libertas contrarietatis, sive specificationis, per quam quis potest agere hoc, aut illud, aut etiam actus contrarios edere, & libertatem contradictionis, sive exercitii, per quam quis saltem potest ab agendo cessare, & actionem suspendere; statuunt esse quandam libertatem complacentiae, quae reperitur in eo qui nulla vi externa adactus, nec etiam ullo caeco & bruto impulsu ductus, sed proprio judicio, ad actionem aliquam movetur, quamvis propter luminis quo ducitur evidentiam, a se impetrare non possit ut contrarium actum eliciat, aut etiam ab illa actione desistat. Quam distinctionem non tantum tradit Gabriel Biel verbis ante allegatis, sed etiam ex recentioribus Johannes Viguerius in Academia Tolosana Theologiae Doctor & Professor. Loquendo, inquit, de indeterminatione, sive libertate voluntatis circa objectum ultimi finis, in patria est omnino determinata, sive non est libera, nec quoad specificationem, neque quoad exercitium: sive non est libera libertate contradictionis, vel contrarietatis; est tamen libera libertate Complacentiae: quia complacet & delectatur in illo objecto. in institutionibus Theologicis cap. 3. §. 3. versu 1.
english: The schools speak of freedom of contrariety or specification, by which one can do this or that, or even perform opposite acts, and of freedom of contradiction or exercise, by which one can at least stop acting and hold the act back.

Beyond these two they set a freedom of complacency, or delight. It is found in someone who is moved to an action neither by outside force nor by blind animal impulse but by his own judgment, even though the light guiding him is so evident that he cannot bring himself to the opposite act or even to leave off the one he is doing.

Gabriel Biel gives this distinction in the words quoted earlier, and so does the more recent John Viguier, doctor and professor of theology at Toulouse. 'As to the will's indeterminacy or freedom regarding its last end,' he says, 'in heaven it is wholly determined and not free, either in specification or in exercise. It lacks the freedom of contradiction and of contrariety, yet it is free with the freedom of complacency, because it takes pleasure and delight in that object.' (Institutiones theologicae, ch. 3, §3, v. 1.)

source_text: XXV. Illum autem qui ex certo rationis judicio agit, sive necessario, sive contingenter agat, existimant agere libere, quoniam semper agit & appetit ad sui ipsius imperium, & sic vult aliquid ut velit se velle illud, suam ipsius voluntatem probans, dum tacite vel expresse supra ipsam reflectitur, & ita in actu volendi seipsum movet, & sibi dominatur, ut loquitur Bonaventura loco super citato. Vel quia, ut ait Scotus, Voluntas propter firmitatem libertatis suae, sibi ipsi necessitatem imponit in eliciendo actum, & in perseverando, sive figendo se in actum. Quodlib. 16.
english: They consider that anyone acting on a settled judgment of reason acts freely, whether he acts necessarily or contingently.

He always acts and seeks under his own command. He wills a thing in such a way that he wills himself to will it, and so approves his own will, turning back on it silently or openly. In this way, in the very act of willing he moves and rules himself, as Bonaventure puts it in the passage cited above.

Or, in Scotus's words, 'the will, through the firmness of its freedom, lays necessity on itself in bringing forth its act and in persevering in it, that is, in fixing itself on the act.' (Quodlibet 16.)
